name: Forth and Bargy dialect / Yola
confidence_why: Every account agrees that Forth and Bargy stressed the last syllable, from the contemporary observers Hore and Russell (1857/58) printed in Poole 1867 to Hickey 2010, who reports that all authors describe final stress on most polysyllables; the evidence is thin only because the dialect is extinct and known from a few nineteenth-century observers, and the fuller treatments by O'Rahilly 1932 and Hickey 1988 and 2007 could not be checked for the exact scope of the rule.

catalog_locator: Barnes's introduction p. 13 (Hore's note; repeated verbatim in the note to the Congratulatory Address, p. 113); Appendix, Russell 1857/58 reprint, pp. 132-133
catalog_quote: [p. 13] Mr. Hore writes that to give any idea of the Forth dialect one must speak slowly, " that the letter a has invariably the same sound, like a in father. Double ee sounds like e in me; and in most words of two syllables the long accent is placed on the last. To follow the English pronunciation completely de- prives the dialect of its peculiarities." ... [Appendix, Russell, pp. 132-133] It is hardly worth while to ad- vert to the principles of pronunciation. Many of them are, in the main, those of all the archaic forms of English ... The hard g and c, the broad soundis of the vowels, the pectdiar powers of the diphthongs, are all very strongly marked in the Forth dialect; and there is a general ten- dency in it to lengthened and drawling accentuation, which cannot fail to be observed. Many of our modem monosyllables appear in Forth in the dissyllable form — "halluf/' *'calluf/' **…

new_statements.quote: All authors, who have concerned themselves with Forth and Bargy, refer to two aspects of the dialect (see remarks in Hogan 1927: 44 and those of Barnes in Dolan and Ó Muirithe 1996: 33ff.): firstly, the slow tempo of speech and secondly, the fact that the stress with most polysyllables fell on the final syllable. The slow tempo would seem to have contributed to the unexpected lengthening of vowels which is suggested by many spellings in the glossaries. The stress on the final syllable of polysyllabic forms also led to lengthening. This would seem to have been conditioned, i.e. it occurred when the final syllable ended in a sonorant: before /n/: za/moon 'salmon', smadde/reen 'smattering', lic/keen 'looking', chi/sool 'chisel', fa/shoon 'fashion', before /r/: wur/gheere 'bellows', wy/ddeer 'furze'.

new_statements.relation_note: Refines the catalog's the rule as stated '01' (final stress in disyllables, from Russell 1857/58 and Hore in Barnes 1867): Hickey generalises the placement to 'most polysyllables' (not only disyllables), i.e. final stress for words of any length, and adds the phonetic detail that the stressed final vowel lengthened before sonorants and in open syllables. Same placement as the catalog and as the Wikipedia/O'Rahilly carrier ('stress shifted to the second syllable' in disyllables = final syllable). new_statements.rule_in_words: In the extinct Forth and Bargy dialect, stress in most polysyllabic words fell on the final syllable (unlike the initial stress of mainstream English); the stressed final vowel was lengthened when the final syllable ended in a sonorant (/n/, /r/) or was open (bellee 'belly'). The final stress also caused procope of an initial unstressed vowel in a few words (garr 'anger', twish 'betwixt'). Hickey presents this as the consensus of all earlier commentators (Hogan 1927: 44; Barnes 1867 in Dolan and Ó Muirithe 1996: 33ff.) and separately notes (p. 10) that 'The Celtologist T. F. O'Rahilly compared the stress system of this dialect with that of surrounding varieties of Irish (O'Rahilly 1932: 94f.)'.
new_statements.exceptions: Hedged as 'most polysyllables'; no exception list. A possible stressed epenthetic vowel in gaudès 'fine clothes', nollès 'awls', oathès 'oats' (grave accent used by the glossarists) is raised but explicitly left unconfirmed ('this cannot be confirmed by evidence from elsewhere').
new_statements.identity_note: All sources concern the extinct English dialect of the baronies of Forth and Bargy, Co. Wexford (Yola; Glottolog east2834 'Irish Anglo-Norman', dialect node yola1237), attested from 18th-19th-century glossaries (Vallancey 1788, Poole/Barnes 1867); the related Fingal variety (fing1234) is mentioned by Hickey but not described for stress. No living speakers; all statements are reconstructions from spellings and contemporary remarks.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement among the readable sources on placement: Russell 1857/58 and Hore (in Barnes 1867, the catalog's primary source) put the accent on the last syllable of disyllables 'almost invariably' / 'in most words of two syllables'; Hickey 2010 extends the same statement to 'most polysyllables'; the Wikipedia carrier of O'Rahilly 1932 says stress 'shifted to the second syllable of words in many instances'. The only open question is scope and strength: the 19th-century witnesses speak of disyllables only, Hickey of polysyllables generally, and O'Rahilly (as carried) hedges 'in many instances'. Whether O'Rahilly frames the shift as conditioned on a long final vowel (which would make the rule weight-sensitive) could not be checked because his chapter is not open.

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.recode_to: No class change. Keep fixed final ('01'); widen the primary-stress rule scope from 'disyllables only' to 'final syllable in most polysyllables (Hickey 2010), near-categorical in disyllables (Russell 1857)', cite Hickey 2010 §2.4 as modern corroboration, and note that Hickey treats final-vowel length as a consequence of final stress (conditioned by a final sonorant or open syllable), which weakens the quantity-sensitive/length-conditioned alternative flagged by a check.
audit.deciding_source_year: 1867 (Hore's note as printed 1867; Russell read 1857, publ. 1858)
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: both deciding sentences are verbatim at the stated pages in the held scanned of Poole 1867 (p. 13 = p. 113 Hore; pp. 132-133 Russell). (2) Deciding source is a 19th-c. glossary edition carrying two lay/antiquarian observations; it is primary and contemporaneous with the last speakers but is not a linguistic analysis, and the dedicated modern treatments (O'Rahilly 1932; Hickey 1988; Hickey 2007 pp. 66-84) are not yet obtained and not open (archive.org lending-only / paywalled, verified from metadata and Hickey's own PDF list).
